title: Eagle Digital Chip
summary: RISC-V LiteX SoC with a custom Cooley-Tukey FFT accelerator.
text: The 2023 C2S2 Digital Tapeout showcases a design centered around a RISC-V Litex System on Chip. This chip features a custom digital Cooley-Tukey Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) implementation, optimized for high-speed signal processing tasks. The RISC-V architecture provides a flexible and scalable processing platform, enabling efficient execution of complex algorithms and data manipulation.
features: RISC-V 32-bit processor core for general-purpose computing
Custom digital Cooley-Tukey FFT hardware accelerator

title: Sparrow Analog Chip
summary: Mixed-signal SoC integrating op-amps, analog interfaces, and a multiplier.
text: The 2023 C2S2 Analog Tapeout features an innovative hardware design centered around a RISC-V Litex System on Chip (SoC). This versatile chip incorporates multiple analog components to enhance its functionality: operational amplifiers – integrated to provide versatile analog signal processing capabilities, 'fingers' implementation – allows for efficient interfacing and control in various analog scenarios, and 'multiplier' implementation – facilitates analog multiplication processes for applications requiring signal modulation and other complex mathematical operations.

specifications.Architecture: RISC-V Litex SoC with Analog Components

features: Integrated operational amplifiers for analog signal processing
Custom 'fingers' implementation for efficient analog interfacing
Analog multiplier for signal modulation applications
Mixed-signal design combining digital processing with analog I/O
RISC-V Litex SoC for control and digital processing

title: Kiwi Analog Chip
summary: A 4-bit Flash ADC and an 8-bit delta-sigma modulator for analog-to-digital conversion.
text: The 2024 C2S2 Analog Tapeout, codename Kiwi, contains a 4-bit Flash ADC and an 8-bit delta-sigma modulator. Both are techniques for discretizing analog signals, such as sound, into digital signals for processing. However, they differ greatly in speed and resolution and therefore target different end-use scenarios. The 4-bit Flash ADC was designed for a speed of 40 MS/s, making it suitable for rapidly converting analog signals at reduced precision. The 8-bit delta-sigma modulator is more suitable for converting lower-speed analog signals into higher-precision digital signals. The delta-sigma modulator did not include a digital demodulator, which made it more difficult to interface with. This issue was addressed in the 2025 ADC.

title: Puffin Digital Chip
summary: RISC-V SoC connecting an FFT sound classifier through a Wishbone bus.
text:
The Spring 24 tapeout builds on top of the Spring 23 tapeout. This is our final iteration of the sound classifier, featuring a 16-bit fixed point (8 integer bits) 32-point Cooley Tukey FFT module, as well as a configurable classifier.

Previously, the RISC-V core and the digital classifier were two isolated blocks on the same tapeout. Puffin is where we bridged the gap between the two blocks by interfacing them with a Wishbone Bus, yielding a more integrated SoC.

specifications.Architecture: RISC-V SoC with Wishbone Bus Integration

features: 16-bit fixed point (8 integer bits) 32-point Cooley-Tukey FFT module
Wishbone Bus interface bridging RISC-V core and digital classifier
More integrated SoC design compared to previous tapeout
Final iteration of the sound classification pipeline

title: Kestrel Analog Chip
summary: An 8-bit SAR ADC optimized for resolution, power, and straightforward digital interfacing.
text: The 2025 C2S2 Analog Tapeout, codename Kestrel, contains an 8-bit SAR ADC (successive-approximation analog-to-digital converter) and several test structures. Similar to the 2024 Kiwi ADC, it converts continuous analog signals, such as audio, temperature, and motion, into discrete digital values for further processing by the digital tapeout. Although it serves a similar purpose, this SAR ADC is more highly optimized for resolution, power, and ease of digital interfacing, targeting battery-powered audio-sampling use cases. The ADC can also be used for medium-speed applications, sampling at 5 MS/s. Its straightforward digital interface gives the ADC IP future potential for integration with a digital chip with little added complexity, enabling higher levels of system integration. Real-world test data confirms that the ADC is fully functional and draws power on the order of microwatts.

specifications.Target Applications: Battery-powered audio sampling and medium-speed sensing

title: Kakapo Analog Chip
summary: Asynchronous SAR ADC, adiabatic comparator, and flash ADC.
text: The 2026 C2S2 Analog Tapeout (codename Kakapo) contains a 3-bit 40 MS/s "Adiabatic" Flash ADC and an 8-bit 4.4 MS/s Asynchronous SAR ADC. The Flash ADC aims to mitigate the relatively high power draw of the Flash topology by leveraging the principles of adiabatic (i.e. reversible) compute for both its analog and digital circuits. This enables extraordinarily low power draw, on the order of several microwatts, while maintaining a relatively high sampling rate. This was the team's first foray into the world of reversible compute. The 8-bit SAR ADC improves upon the SAR ADC from Kestrel, utilizing self-timing to remove time segments in the ADC's convergence process that would otherwise remain unused. This required a digital logic redesign, as well as the addition of a variable delay line to enable self-timing. Importantly, this asynchronous ADC enables a faster sampling rate than the previous SAR without requiring a redesign of every major component. The tapeout also includes chip art of a kākāpō bird (the chip's namesake), the names of the analog subteam members who designed the chip, and the logos of the team and its sponsors.

title: Seneca-1 RFIC Transceiver
text: Seneca-1 is C2S2’s Spring 2026 RFIC tapeout and the team’s first transceiver at 2.4 GHz, moving up from previous RFIC designs at 915 MHz. It implements a simple half-duplex on-off keying (OOK) radio in TSMC 180 nm, meaning it sends and receives data by switching a 2.4 GHz carrier on and off. The transmitter is a differential Class-F power amplifier. Class-F was chosen because OOK does not require a linear amplifier, so the design could prioritize efficiency instead; it is designed to support both a low-power mode for OOK and a higher-power mode. The receiver chain consists of a low-noise amplifier, a cascode pre-amplifier, an envelope detector, and a comparator, which together take a weak incoming signal and convert it directly into digital bits. The chip also includes a temperature-compensated current reference to keep each RF block biased consistently as temperature changes. The higher-power transmit mode was designed with constant-envelope modulation in mind, which ties directly into this year’s 2.4 GHz FSK transceiver. Seneca-1 has been fabricated, and testing is currently underway.

specifications.Receiver: Low-noise amplifier, cascode pre-amplifier, envelope detector, comparator
